title: A transition marker is direction-neutral continuation rather than an endpoint verb
summary: GDT769 reports mixed-direction state bridges for otar and a supported continuation rival. The hypothesis is a reversible continuation relation that composes both forward and backward record transitions.

design.unit: source-bound complete records or visual-text contexts named in source_observation
design.prediction: the same form should occur in both transition directions without changing the relation; an endpoint model predicts a stable rightward attained state
design.countermodel: This is near existing operator ideas, but the committed contrast is reversibility under direction, not generic “then”.
design.falsifier: A form assigned as continuation is confined to one direction or consistently precedes a terminal state.
design.principal_risk: No independent event ordering gold; source line boundaries are not clause gold.

evidence.quote:
### `otar`: R05 step transition, not `bis`

Of 110 exact `otar` occurrences on 55 pages, 105 are medial. Four clean state bridges run in mixed directions rather than repeatedly pointing toward one endpoint. In `f86v5.13`, `otar` follows a complete amount expression and opens the next value field; in `f75r.43`, it sits between a state block and a repeated close/result form; in `f115v.5`, it directly precedes an independent process word. A general `dann/anschließend/weiter` survives all three uses better than a specific material or process term.

The local frames make `weiter/dann` a useful reader default, but R05 and R01 both pass with the same score of 1.0. R05 is selected only by specificity priority, so the nominal preparation/record field remains the principal supported role rival. Confidence is `C1_LOCAL_FRAME__C0_ROLE_TIEBREAK`. At identity level, `bis` is now the primary rival: mixed transition directions make it less portable than a general continuation marker, but do not eliminate it. No lexical identity is confirmed.

design.smallest_test: Use the three named GDT769 otar frames plus one held frame; classify direction and endpoint only, keeping all lexical identities open.
